issues.legal_issue: A public statutory body that receives special treatment from rent-control law must act in the public interest when dealing with its tenants, and its actions are subject to judicial review.
material_facts: The Port Trust was a statutory public authority and was exempt from the operation of the rent-control statute.
The dispute concerned the Port Trust’s termination of a tenant’s tenancy and its decision to let the premises to another occupant.
issues.conclusion: The Port Trust’s dealings with tenants were required to serve the public interest, and an alleged failure to meet that duty was reviewable in a civil suit or writ jurisdiction.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 12 and 14 of the Constitution require State action to be reasonable and based on lawful, relevant grounds of public interest, including in contractual dealings. The exemption under Section 4 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1947, rested on the expectation that public authorities would not act like private landlords. The Court relied on Rampratap Jaidayal v. Dominion of India, Baburao Shantaram More v. Bombay Housing Board, Radhakrishna Agarwal v. State of Bihar, LIC v. Escorts Ltd., S.P. Rekhi v. Union of India, M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu, Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, R.D. Shetty v. International Airport Authority of India, Kasturi Lal Lakshmi Reddy v. State of Jammu and Kashmir, and Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib Sehravardi.

predicates.public_statutory_body: A public statutory authority carried out the relevant action.
predicates.tenant_dealing: The authority dealt with a person who occupied its property as a tenant.
predicates.special_rent_law_exemption: The authority was exempt from ordinary rent-control protections on account of its public character.

issues.definition: When a public statutory authority exempt from ordinary rent-control protections deals with a tenant, that dealing must serve the public interest and is subject to review.

issues.legal_issue: A court reviewing a public authority’s tenant-allocation decision may assess whether the decision-making process followed a reasonable policy serving a public purpose, but may not substitute a different decision merely because it considers that decision better.
material_facts: A town-planning scheme reconstituted and divided the land, and the Port Trust sought to develop the resulting plot in accordance with that scheme.
One occupant held the major portion of the reconstituted plot, and the Port Trust followed a policy of allocating the entire plot to the major occupant for development.
The appellant’s portion was smaller, and the proposed joint development was not shown to be feasible; the plot allocated to a major occupant was developed.
The appellant challenged its eviction and the allocation as inconsistent with public interest and the Port Trust’s policy.
issues.conclusion: The Port Trust’s decision was not improper: its policy was referable to public purpose, and the Court would not replace that decision with a different allocation merely because another policy might have been preferable.
issues.legal_principle: State action must be reasonable and informed by public interest, and the challenger bears a heavy burden to show that it is arbitrary, unreasonable, contrary to professed norms, or not informed by public interest. Judicial review examines the decision-making process, not whether the court would have made a better decision. The Court relied on Articles 14 and 227 of the Constitution; Sections 2, 13, 14, 22, 59, 65, 88, 89, 159 and 169 of the relevant town-planning legislation; and Council of Civil Service Unions v. Minister for the Civil Service, Chief Constable of the North Wales Police v. Evans, In re Preston v. IRC, Regina v. Chief Constable of the Merseyside Police, Kasturi Lal Lakshmi Reddy v. State of Jammu and Kashmir, and R.D. Shetty v. International Airport Authority of India.

rule.if: public_authority_tenant_eviction_challenge and reconstituted_land_required_development and policy_allocated_plot_to_major_occupant and allocation_served_public_purpose

predicates.public_authority_tenant_eviction_challen: A tenant challenged a public authority’s decision to terminate the tenancy and allocate the property to another occupant.
predicates.reconstituted_land_required_development: A planning scheme reconstituted the land and made development of the resulting plot relevant to the allocation decision.
predicates.policy_allocated_plot_to_major_occupant: The authority followed a policy of allocating the whole reconstituted plot to the occupant holding the major portion.
predicates.allocation_served_public_purpose: The allocation policy was connected to development of the land for a public purpose.

issues.definition: When a tenant challenges an eviction and allocation decision made under a development scheme, an allocation under a public-purpose policy favoring the major occupant is not invalidated merely because a different policy might have been better.

issues.legal_issue: A challenge to a tenancy-termination notice that would require factual reappraisal is not reopened when the reviewing courts have upheld the notice and the available appellate review does not permit that reappraisal.
material_facts: The tenant argued that the tenancy was for a manufacturing purpose and that the termination notice was invalid, and also disputed whether the notice had been waived.
The trial court and appellate court reached differing conclusions on the notice, but the High Court upheld the appellate court’s finding that the notice was valid and had not been waived.
The Supreme Court stated that the High Court was right on this aspect and that the matter could not be reappraised in the appeal.
issues.conclusion: The finding that the termination notice was valid and had not been waived was not reopened in the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the High Court could not have gone into this question under Article 227 in the circumstances, and that the Supreme Court could not reappraise it in an appeal under Article 136.

predicates.appeal_from_tenant_eviction: The proceeding was an appeal concerning an order for eviction of a tenant.
predicates.reviewing_court_upheld_valid_notice: The reviewing court upheld a finding that the termination notice was valid and had not been waived.
predicates.deciding_challenge_requires_factual_reap: Resolving the challenge would require the appellate court to reappraise the underlying factual findings.

issues.definition: In an eviction appeal, a finding upholding a termination notice is not reopened when reconsidering it would require factual reappraisal.
